claim: Loss of function of the X-linked gene encoding methyl-CpG binding protein 2 (MeCP2) causes the progressive neurological disorder Rett syndrome (RTT).
source: Loss of function of the X-linked gene encoding methyl-CpG binding protein 2 (MeCP2) causes the progressive neurological disorder Rett syndrome (RTT).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the genetic cause of Rett syndrome, supported by the citation (Amir et al., 1999) in the Introduction.

claim: Duplication or triplication of Xq28 causes MECP2 duplication syndrome, a progressive neurological disorder whose features overlap somewhat with RTT.
source: Conversely, duplication or triplication of Xq28 causes an equally wide-ranging progressive neurological disorder, MECP2 duplication syndrome, whose features overlap somewhat with RTT.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MECP2 duplication syndrome, supported by multiple citations in the Introduction (del Gaudio et al., 2006; Friez et al., 2006; Lugtenberg et al., 2006; Meins et al., 2005; Van Esch et al., 2005).

claim: Both the MBD and TRD must function for doubling MeCP2 to be toxic.
source: We determined that both the MBD and TRD must function for doubling MeCP2 to be toxic.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by behavioral and survival data from R111G Tg and R306C Tg mice showing no phenotypes.

claim: Mutating the MBD reproduces the null phenotype.
source: Mutating the MBD reproduces the null phenotype and expressing the TRD mutant produces milder RTT phenotypes, yet both mutations are harmless when expressed with endogenous Mecp2.
evidence: This is supported by survival data showing R111G mice die as prematurely as null mice (Figure 2A).

claim: Expressing the TRD mutant produces milder RTT phenotypes.
source: Mutating the MBD reproduces the null phenotype and expressing the TRD mutant produces milder RTT phenotypes, yet both mutations are harmless when expressed with endogenous Mecp2.
evidence: This is supported by survival and behavioral data showing R306C mice have intermediate phenotypes between WT and null (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: Both R111G and R306C mutations are harmless when expressed with endogenous Mecp2.
source: Mutating the MBD reproduces the null phenotype and expressing the TRD mutant produces milder RTT phenotypes, yet both mutations are harmless when expressed with endogenous Mecp2.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral and survival data showing R111G Tg and R306C Tg mice are indistinguishable from WT (Figures 2 and 4).

claim: Mutating the TRD is more detrimental than deleting the entire C-terminus.
source: Surprisingly, mutating the TRD is more detrimental than deleting the entire C-terminus, indicating a dominant-negative effect on MeCP2 function, likely due to the disruption of a basic cluster.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of survival data: R306C mice have median survival of 18 weeks versus G273X mice with 28 weeks (Figure 7A).

claim: The R306C mutation has a dominant-negative effect on MeCP2 function, likely due to the disruption of a basic cluster.
source: Surprisingly, mutating the TRD is more detrimental than deleting the entire C-terminus, indicating a dominant-negative effect on MeCP2 function, likely due to the disruption of a basic cluster.
evidence: This is inferred from ChIP and EMSA data showing R306C reduces DNA binding more than G273X truncation (Figure 7B-C).

claim: After a 6- to 18-month period of normal development, head growth slows in RTT-affected girls.
source: After a 6- to 18-month period of normal development, head growth slows and affected girls lose acquired speech, dexterity, and social skills; they then develop characteristic hand stereotypies, respiratory dysrhythmias, seizures, and autistic-like features (Hagberg et al., 1983; Lam et al., 2000; Klauck et al., 2002; Carney et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about RTT progression, supported by multiple citations.

claim: RTT-affected girls lose acquired speech, dexterity, and social skills.
source: After a 6- to 18-month period of normal development, head growth slows and affected girls lose acquired speech, dexterity, and social skills; they then develop characteristic hand stereotypies, respiratory dysrhythmias, seizures, and autistic-like features (Hagberg et al., 1983; Lam et al., 2000; Klauck et al., 2002; Carney et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about RTT symptoms, supported by multiple citations.

claim: RTT-affected girls develop characteristic hand stereotypies, respiratory dysrhythmias, seizures, and autistic-like features.
source: After a 6- to 18-month period of normal development, head growth slows and affected girls lose acquired speech, dexterity, and social skills; they then develop characteristic hand stereotypies, respiratory dysrhythmias, seizures, and autistic-like features (Hagberg et al., 1983; Lam et al., 2000; Klauck et al., 2002; Carney et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about RTT symptoms, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Children with MECP2 duplication syndrome present with infantile hypotonia.
source: Children with the duplication syndrome present with infantile hypotonia and develop severe intellectual disability, autistic-like features, recurrent respiratory infections, spasticity, seizures, and premature lethality (del Gaudio et al., 2006; Friez et al., 2006; Lugtenberg et al., 2006; Meins et al., 2005; Van Esch et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about MECP2 duplication syndrome, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Children with MECP2 duplication syndrome develop severe intellectual disability, autistic-like features, recurrent respiratory infections, spasticity, seizures, and premature lethality.
source: Children with the duplication syndrome present with infantile hypotonia and develop severe intellectual disability, autistic-like features, recurrent respiratory infections, spasticity, seizures, and premature lethality (del Gaudio et al., 2006; Friez et al., 2006; Lugtenberg et al., 2006; Meins et al., 2005; Van Esch et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about MECP2 duplication syndrome, supported by multiple citations.

claim: MeCP2 was first identified over 20 years ago as a transcriptional repressor that binds to methylated CpG dinucleotides.
source: MeCP2 was first identified over 20 years ago as a transcriptional repressor that binds to methylated CpG dinucleotides (Lewis et al., 1992; Wakefield et al., 1999; Free et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MeCP2 function, supported by citations.

claim: MeCP2 binds DNA directly through its N-terminal methyl-CpG binding domain (MBD).
source: It binds DNA directly through its N-terminal methyl-CpG binding domain (MBD), whereas its C-terminal transcriptional repression domain (TRD) allows it to interact with corepressors such as Sin3a, HDAC1, and HDAC2 (Nan et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MeCP2 structure and function, supported by citation.

claim: MeCP2's C-terminal transcriptional repression domain (TRD) allows it to interact with corepressors such as Sin3a, HDAC1, and HDAC2.
source: It binds DNA directly through its N-terminal methyl-CpG binding domain (MBD), whereas its C-terminal transcriptional repression domain (TRD) allows it to interact with corepressors such as Sin3a, HDAC1, and HDAC2 (Nan et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MeCP2 function, supported by citation.

claim: MeCP2 is expressed at higher levels than expected for classical site-specific transcriptional repressors.
source: More recent work has revealed that MeCP2 is expressed at higher levels than expected for classical site-specific transcriptional repressors: it binds as abundantly and widely throughout the genome as histone H1, which suggests MeCP2 might have additional functions in chromatin biology (Nan et al., 1997; Skene et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing MeCP2 abundance.

claim: MeCP2 binds as abundantly and widely throughout the genome as histone H1.
source: More recent work has revealed that MeCP2 is expressed at higher levels than expected for classical site-specific transcriptional repressors: it binds as abundantly and widely throughout the genome as histone H1, which suggests MeCP2 might have additional functions in chromatin biology (Nan et al., 1997; Skene et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing MeCP2 genome-wide binding.

claim: MeCP2 might have additional functions in chromatin biology beyond transcriptional repression.
source: More recent work has revealed that MeCP2 is expressed at higher levels than expected for classical site-specific transcriptional repressors: it binds as abundantly and widely throughout the genome as histone H1, which suggests MeCP2 might have additional functions in chromatin biology (Nan et al., 1997; Skene et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation based on MeCP2's abundance and binding pattern.

claim: Most genes are downregulated in RTT models that lack MeCP2.
source: Further complicating the picture of MeCP2 function are transcriptional studies in mouse brains as well as human embryonic stem cell-derived neurons, which have shown that most genes are actually downregulated in RTT models that lack MeCP2 (Chahrour et al., 2008; Ben-Shachar et al., 2009; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to transcriptional studies.

claim: MeCP2 acts as a 'transcriptional noise dampener', such that loss of MeCP2 function results in the diversion of basal transcriptional machinery to repetitive elements, indirectly leading to global transcriptional downregulation.
source: One proposal to explain this is that MeCP2 acts as a 'transcriptional noise dampener', such that loss of MeCP2 function results in the diversion of basal transcriptional machinery to repetitive elements, indirectly leading to global transcriptional downregulation (Skene et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in the cited study.

claim: The same genes that are downregulated in RTT models are upregulated in MECP2 duplication syndrome mouse models with double the MeCP2 expression.
source: Additional transcriptional studies present a challenge for this hypothesis, however, as the same genes that are downregulated in the RTT models are upregulated in MECP2 duplication syndrome mouse models with double the MeCP2 expression (Chahrour et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a transcriptional study.

claim: Most RTT-causing mutations disrupt either the MBD or TRD.
source: Because most RTT-causing mutations disrupt either the MBD or TRD, we decided to use a genetic approach to determine how these regions might be involved in mediating the toxicity observed in MECP2 duplication syndrome models.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RTT mutations.

claim: The R111G mutation replaces an arginine with a glycine at residue 111 and is a RTT-causing point mutation.
source: To explore the role of the MBD in RTT and MECP2 duplication syndrome, we chose a RTT-causing point mutation that replaces an arginine with a glycine at residue 111 (R111G) (Laccone et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study identifying this mutation.

claim: R111 is critical for methyl-CpG binding in vitro.
source: R111 is critical for methyl-CpG binding in vitro: when it is mutated (R111G), it completely abolishes binding to methyl-CpGs in vitro without affecting the structure of the MBD or the rest of the protein (Free et al., 2001; Kudo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claim: The R111G mutation completely abolishes binding to methyl-CpGs in vitro without affecting the structure of the MBD or the rest of the protein.
source: R111 is critical for methyl-CpG binding in vitro: when it is mutated (R111G), it completely abolishes binding to methyl-CpGs in vitro without affecting the structure of the MBD or the rest of the protein (Free et al., 2001; Kudo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claim: The mutation of arginine to cysteine at residue 306 (R306C) is the second most common RTT-causing missense mutation.
source: In fact, the mutation of arginine to cysteine at residue 306 (R306C) is the second most common RTT-causing missense mutation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RTT mutations, supported by citation (Christodoulou et al., 2003) in the text.

claim: The R306C mutation abolishes interaction with the NCoR corepressor complex.
source: Although recent studies have shown that the R306C mutation abolishes interaction with the NCoR corepressor complex, a mouse model bearing a truncated form of MeCP2 that lacks the NCoR binding site has a milder phenotype than the published mice carrying the R306C mutation, indicating that R306C has other effects on the function of MeCP2 (Baker et al., 2013; Ebert et al., 2013; Lyst et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: A mouse model bearing a truncated form of MeCP2 that lacks the NCoR binding site has a milder phenotype than the published mice carrying the R306C mutation.
source: Although recent studies have shown that the R306C mutation abolishes interaction with the NCoR corepressor complex, a mouse model bearing a truncated form of MeCP2 that lacks the NCoR binding site has a milder phenotype than the published mice carrying the R306C mutation, indicating that R306C has other effects on the function of MeCP2 (Baker et al., 2013; Ebert et al., 2013; Lyst et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies comparing mouse models.

claim: R306C has other effects on the function of MeCP2 beyond abolishing NCoR interaction.
source: Although recent studies have shown that the R306C mutation abolishes interaction with the NCoR corepressor complex, a mouse model bearing a truncated form of MeCP2 that lacks the NCoR binding site has a milder phenotype than the published mice carrying the R306C mutation, indicating that R306C has other effects on the function of MeCP2 (Baker et al., 2013; Ebert et al., 2013; Lyst et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of phenotypes between different mouse models.

claim: Two independent lines of MeCP2-R111G express transgenic MeCP2 at levels similar to those of endogenous MeCP2, thus doubling the total MeCP2 level.
source: After establishing transgenic lines for each mutation, we characterized the protein levels of two independent lines for each mutation by western blot and found that they expressed transgenic MeCP2 at levels similar to those of endogenous MeCP2, thus doubling the total MeCP2 level (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Two independent lines of MeCP2-R306C express transgenic MeCP2 at levels similar to those of endogenous MeCP2, thus doubling the total MeCP2 level.
source: After establishing transgenic lines for each mutation, we characterized the protein levels of two independent lines for each mutation by western blot and found that they expressed transgenic MeCP2 at levels similar to those of endogenous MeCP2, thus doubling the total MeCP2 level (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The distribution pattern of transgenic MeCP2 parallels that of endogenous MeCP2 throughout the whole brain.
source: Immunofluorescence using anti-MeCP2 and anti-GFP antibodies on midsagittal sections of the whole brain shows that the distribution pattern of transgenic MeCP2 parallels that of endogenous MeCP2 (Figure 1C, upper panel).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Transgenic and endogenous MeCP2 colocalize in the cortex and cerebellum.
source: This colocalization also holds true upon closer inspection of the cortex and cerebellum (Figure 1C, lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mecp2 null mice started displaying symptoms around 4–6 weeks of age.
source: Mecp2 null mice started displaying symptoms around 4–6 weeks of age and had a median lifespan of 11 weeks (Guy et al., 2001) (Figure 2A, red line), and the R111G mice died as prematurely as the null mice (Figure 2A, green line).
evidence: This is supported by citation and survival data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mecp2 null mice had a median lifespan of 11 weeks.
source: Mecp2 null mice started displaying symptoms around 4–6 weeks of age and had a median lifespan of 11 weeks (Guy et al., 2001) (Figure 2A, red line), and the R111G mice died as prematurely as the null mice (Figure 2A, green line).
evidence: This is supported by citation and survival data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: R111G mice died as prematurely as the null mice.
source: Mecp2 null mice started displaying symptoms around 4–6 weeks of age and had a median lifespan of 11 weeks (Guy et al., 2001) (Figure 2A, red line), and the R111G mice died as prematurely as the null mice (Figure 2A, green line).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The R111G mutation disrupts a critical function of MeCP2, such that it becomes effectively a null allele.
source: This indicates that the R111G mutation disrupts a critical function of MeCP2, such that it becomes effectively a null allele.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival data showing R111G mice phenocopy null mice.

claim: R111G Tg mice have a normal lifespan.
source: Although the R111G Tg had a lifespan like the WT and appeared normal, we wanted to determine if they had any subtle behavioral deficits.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Older mice expressing two functional copies of MeCP2 exhibit mild phenotypes, such as hypoactivity, reduced anxiety, and improved learning.
source: Older mice expressing two functional copies of MeCP2 exhibit mild phenotypes, such as hypoactivity, reduced anxiety, and improved learning (Collins et al., 2004; Na et al., 2012), so we aged the WT and R111G Tg mice to 9 months before starting our battery of behavioral tests.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in distance traveled in the open field assay.
source: We found no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in any of these behaviors (Figure 2B–I), indicating that an intact MBD is necessary to elicit the toxicity seen in the duplication syndrome model.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There is no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in the center-to-total ratio in the open field assay.
source: We found no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in any of these behaviors (Figure 2B–I), indicating that an intact MBD is necessary to elicit the toxicity seen in the duplication syndrome model.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There is no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in time spent in the dark in the light/dark assay.
source: We found no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in any of these behaviors (Figure 2B–I), indicating that an intact MBD is necessary to elicit the toxicity seen in the duplication syndrome model.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in rotarod performance.
source: We found no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in any of these behaviors (Figure 2B–I), indicating that an intact MBD is necessary to elicit the toxicity seen in the duplication syndrome model.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There is no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in footslips per distance traveled in parallel rod footslip.
source: We found no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in any of these behaviors (Figure 2B–I), indicating that an intact MBD is necessary to elicit the toxicity seen in the duplication syndrome model.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There is no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in nest building after 24 hr.
source: We found no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in any of these behaviors (Figure 2B–I), indicating that an intact MBD is necessary to elicit the toxicity seen in the duplication syndrome model.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: There is no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in contextual conditioned fear test.
source: We found no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in any of these behaviors (Figure 2B–I), indicating that an intact MBD is necessary to elicit the toxicity seen in the duplication syndrome model.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: There is no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in cued conditioned fear test.
source: We found no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in any of these behaviors (Figure 2B–I), indicating that an intact MBD is necessary to elicit the toxicity seen in the duplication syndrome model.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: An intact MBD is necessary to elicit the toxicity seen in the duplication syndrome model.
source: We found no difference between WT and R111G Tg mice in any of these behaviors (Figure 2B–I), indicating that an intact MBD is necessary to elicit the toxicity seen in the duplication syndrome model.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of phenotypes in R111G Tg mice.

claim: The phenotypes of the R111G mice are exclusively caused by the mutation, and not insertional effects of the transgene.
source: These data also show that the phenotypes of the R111G mice (when the only MeCP2 allele is mutated) are exclusively caused by the mutation, and not insertional effects of the transgene, as the presence of a WT MeCP2 allele (in the R111G Tg mice) displays no phenotypes.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of R111G and R111G Tg phenotypes.

claim: MeCP2-R111G is unable to localize to heterochromatic foci.
source: We found that MeCP2-R111G was unable to localize to heterochromatic foci (Figure 3A, lower panel), suggesting it is unable to bind methyl-CpGs in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MeCP2-R111G is unable to bind methyl-CpGs in vivo.
source: We found that MeCP2-R111G was unable to localize to heterochromatic foci (Figure 3A, lower panel), suggesting it is unable to bind methyl-CpGs in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of localization to heterochromatic foci.

claim: MeCP2-R111G retained the ability to interact with both Sin3a and NCoR corepressor complexes to the same degree as MeCP2-EGFP.
source: As expected, MeCP2-R111G retained the ability to interact with both corepressor complexes to the same degree as MeCP2-EGFP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The R111G mutation does not affect the ability of MeCP2 to bind corepressors, despite the fact that it disrupts binding to methyl-CpGs.
source: This demonstrates that the R111G mutation does not affect the ability of MeCP2 to bind corepressors, despite the fact that it disrupts binding to methyl-CpGs.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunoprecipitation data showing retained corepressor binding.

claim: R306C Tg mice were indistinguishable from their wild-type littermates by weight, lifespan, and brain size.
source: As with the R111G Tg mice, the R306C Tg mice were indistinguishable from their wild-type littermates by weight, lifespan, and brain size (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4A-C.

claim: R306C mice displayed a milder phenotype than the Mecp2 null mice.
source: The R306C mice, however, displayed a milder phenotype than the Mecp2 null mice.
evidence: This is supported by survival, weight, and behavioral data comparing R306C and null mice.

claim: R306C mice had a median survival of 18 weeks.
source: This milder phenotype was also reflected in the survival (Figure 4A) and weight (Figure 4B) curves: the null mice died early, with a median survival of 11 weeks (Figure 4A, red line) and were severely overweight (Figure 4B, red line), but the R306C mice had a median survival of 18 weeks (Figure 4A, green line) and were mildly overweight (Figure 4B, green line).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: R306C mice were mildly overweight.
source: This milder phenotype was also reflected in the survival (Figure 4A) and weight (Figure 4B) curves: the null mice died early, with a median survival of 11 weeks (Figure 4A, red line) and were severely overweight (Figure 4B, red line), but the R306C mice had a median survival of 18 weeks (Figure 4A, green line) and were mildly overweight (Figure 4B, green line).
evidence: This is supported by weight data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both R306C and null mice had smaller brains, mirroring the microcephaly seen in RTT patients.
source: Both R306C and null mice had smaller brains, mirroring the microcephaly seen in RTT patients (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by brain weight data shown in Figure 4C and comparison to clinical knowledge.

claim: Localization of ATRX to heterochromatic foci is a cell-autonomous marker of disease progression in RTT mouse models.
source: Localization of Alpha Thalassemia/Mental Retardation Syndrome X-Linked (ATRX) to heterochromatic foci has recently been demonstrated to be a cell-autonomous marker of disease progression in other RTT mouse models (Baker et al., 2013), so we evaluated ATRX localization using IF on comparable sections of the CA1, CA2, and CA3 regions of the hippocampus from 7-week-old mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The number of ATRX-positive foci per cell and focus intensity appeared to be the same in WT and R306C Tg.
source: The number of ATRX-positive foci per cell and focus intensity appeared to be the same in WT and R306C Tg (Figure 4D, upper two panels and quantification to the right).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Null mice had the fewest ATRX-positive foci per cell and the lowest focus intensity.
source: Null mice had the fewest ATRX-positive foci per cell and the lowest focus intensity, and R306C mice had an intermediate number of ATRX-positive foci per cell and focus intensity (Figure 4D, lower two panels and quantification to the right).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: R306C mice had an intermediate number of ATRX-positive foci per cell and focus intensity.
source: Null mice had the fewest ATRX-positive foci per cell and the lowest focus intensity, and R306C mice had an intermediate number of ATRX-positive foci per cell and focus intensity (Figure 4D, lower two panels and quantification to the right).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: At 5 weeks of age, R306C Tg mice were indistinguishable from WT mice.
source: At both 5 and 11 weeks, the R306C Tg mice were indistinguishable from WT mice (Figure 5, comparing blue to black).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5.

claim: At 11 weeks of age, R306C Tg mice were indistinguishable from WT mice.
source: At both 5 and 11 weeks, the R306C Tg mice were indistinguishable from WT mice (Figure 5, comparing blue to black).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5.

claim: At 5 weeks of age, R306C and null mice exhibited increased anxiety, as measured by increased time spent in the dark in the light/dark assay.
source: In contrast, at 5 weeks of age, R306C and null mice exhibited increased anxiety, as measured by increased time spent in the dark in the light/dark assay (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At 5 weeks of age, R306C and null mice displayed poor nest building.
source: They displayed poor nest building (Figure 5B) and increased footslips per distance traveled in parallel rod footslip (Figure 5C), indicating deficits in purposeful paw movements and motor dysfunction.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At 5 weeks of age, R306C and null mice showed increased footslips per distance traveled in parallel rod footslip, indicating deficits in purposeful paw movements and motor dysfunction.
source: They displayed poor nest building (Figure 5B) and increased footslips per distance traveled in parallel rod footslip (Figure 5C), indicating deficits in purposeful paw movements and motor dysfunction.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At 5 weeks of age, R306C and null mice showed learning and memory deficits as assayed by freezing in the contextual and cued conditioned fear assay.
source: They also showed learning and memory deficits as assayed by freezing in the contextual and cued conditioned fear assay (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 5D-E.

claim: In all tests at 5 weeks, R306C mice had a less severe phenotype than the null mice.
source: Notably, in all tests, R306C mice had a less severe phenotype than the null mice.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of behavioral data between R306C and null mice.

claim: By 11 weeks of age, R306C mice had become hypoactive as measured by distance traveled in the open field assay.
source: By 11 weeks of age, R306C mice had become hypoactive as measured by distance traveled in the open field assay (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: At 11 weeks of age, R306C mice continued to exhibit anxiety as demonstrated by their decreased time spent in the center in the open field assay.
source: They continued to exhibit anxiety as demonstrated by their decreased time spent in the center in the open field assay (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: At 11 weeks of age, R306C mice's motor dysfunction worsened.
source: Their motor dysfunction worsened (Figure 5H), as did their learning and memory deficits (Figure 5I–J).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: At 11 weeks of age, R306C mice's learning and memory deficits worsened.
source: Their motor dysfunction worsened (Figure 5H), as did their learning and memory deficits (Figure 5I–J).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 5I-J.

claim: Older R306C Tg mice have no motor coordination phenotype, as demonstrated by their ability to stay on a rotating rod in the rotarod assay similarly to WT.
source: Additionally, a new 5-month old cohort showed that older R306C Tg mice have no motor coordination phenotype, as demonstrated by their ability to stay on a rotating rod in the rotarod assay similarly to WT (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: The R306C Tg mice displayed no phenotypes, indicating that the TRD and C-terminus must be intact to observe the toxic effects of doubling MeCP2.
source: In summary, the R306C Tg mice displayed no phenotypes, indicating that the TRD and C-terminus must be intact to observe the toxic effects of doubling MeCP2.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of phenotypes in R306C Tg mice.

claim: The R306C mouse model is a reliable model of RTT that can be used for future studies.
source: Mice carrying the RTT-causing R306C mutation recapitulated many of the phenotypes seen in RTT, including learning and memory deficits and motor dysfunction, indicating that this mouse model is a reliable model of RTT that can be used for future studies.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic similarity between R306C mice and RTT symptoms.

claim: The phenotypes observed in the R306C mice are caused by the mutation and not insertional effects of the transgene.
source: As with the R111G Tg mice, the absence of phenotypes in the R306C Tg mice demonstrates that the phenotypes observed in the R306C mice are caused by the mutation and not insertional effects of the transgene.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of R306C and R306C Tg phenotypes.

claim: MeCP2-R306C retains the ability to bind methyl-CpGs in vivo in a fashion similar to endogenous MeCP2.
source: We performed IF to visualize heterochromatic foci as before and confirmed that MeCP2-R306C retains the ability to bind methyl-CpGs in vivo in a fashion similar to endogenous MeCP2 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MeCP2-R306C bound Sin3a, HDAC1, and HDAC2 similarly to WT EGFP-tagged MeCP2.
source: We found, to our surprise, that MeCP2-R306C bound Sin3a, HDAC1, and HDAC2 similarly to WT EGFP-tagged MeCP2 (Figure 6B, upper half).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: R306C greatly reduces interaction with HDAC3 and Tbl1 of the NCoR corepressor complex.
source: In agreement with a recent study (Lyst et al., 2013), we found that R306C greatly reduces interaction with HDAC3 and Tbl1 of the NCoR corepressor complex (Figure 6B, lower half).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B and citation to a recent study.

claim: The median lifespan of R306C mice (18 weeks) is much shorter than that of G273X mice (28 weeks).
source: However, the median lifespan of R306C mice (18 weeks, this study, Lyst et al., 2013) is much shorter than that of G273X mice (28 weeks, Baker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of survival data from this study and cited studies, shown in Figure 7A.

claim: MeCP2-R306C localized to the promoters of major satellite, L1 retrotransposons, somatostatin (Sst), afamin (Afm), corticotropin releasing hormone (Crh), and Gapdh, but bound to a lesser extent than MeCP2-G273X.
source: We found that MeCP2-R306C localized to the promoters of major satellite, L1 retrotransposons, somatostatin (Sst), afamin (Afm), corticotropin releasing hormone (Crh), and Gapdh, but bound to a lesser extent than MeCP2-G273X (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The WT C-terminal fragment of MeCP2 can bind DNA.
source: An electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) using increasing amounts of N-terminally GST-tagged C-terminal human MeCP2 recombinant protein (amino acids 274–340, from left to right: WT, R306C, R306H, K304E) shows that the WT C-terminal fragment of MeCP2 can bind DNA and that RTT-causing mutations altering the charge of basic residues in the fragment abolish this binding.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: RTT-causing mutations altering the charge of basic residues in the C-terminal fragment abolish DNA binding.
source: An electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) using increasing amounts of N-terminally GST-tagged C-terminal human MeCP2 recombinant protein (amino acids 274–340, from left to right: WT, R306C, R306H, K304E) shows that the WT C-terminal fragment of MeCP2 can bind DNA and that RTT-causing mutations altering the charge of basic residues in the fragment abolish this binding.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The R306C mutation completely abolished the ability of the C-terminal fragment to bind DNA.
source: The WT MeCP2 fragment binds to the double-stranded DNA probe with increasing amount of protein, but the R306C mutation completely abolished the ability of the fragment to bind DNA (Figure 7C, two left panels).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The R306H mutation abolishes the ability of the C-terminal fragment to bind DNA.
source: We further confirmed the importance of the basic cluster flanking R306 by performing EMSAs with two other RTT-causing point mutations: arginine to histidine at residue 306 (R306H) and lysine to glutamic acid at residue 304 (K304E), both of which remove a basic charge from the cluster (Christodoulou et al., 2003). These two mutations also abolish the ability of the fragment to bind DNA (Figure 7C, two right panels), thus emphasizing the importance of the basic cluster in C-terminal DNA binding.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The K304E mutation abolishes the ability of the C-terminal fragment to bind DNA.
source: We further confirmed the importance of the basic cluster flanking R306 by performing EMSAs with two other RTT-causing point mutations: arginine to histidine at residue 306 (R306H) and lysine to glutamic acid at residue 304 (K304E), both of which remove a basic charge from the cluster (Christodoulou et al., 2003). These two mutations also abolish the ability of the fragment to bind DNA (Figure 7C, two right panels), thus emphasizing the importance of the basic cluster in C-terminal DNA binding.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The basic cluster flanking R306 is important for C-terminal DNA binding.
source: We further confirmed the importance of the basic cluster flanking R306 by performing EMSAs with two other RTT-causing point mutations: arginine to histidine at residue 306 (R306H) and lysine to glutamic acid at residue 304 (K304E), both of which remove a basic charge from the cluster (Christodoulou et al., 2003). These two mutations also abolish the ability of the fragment to bind DNA (Figure 7C, two right panels), thus emphasizing the importance of the basic cluster in C-terminal DNA binding.
evidence: This is inferred from EMSA data showing mutations in the basic cluster abolish DNA binding.

claim: The disruption of the basic cluster in MeCP2-R306C reduces binding to DNA even more than the complete absence of the cluster in MeCP2-G273X.
source: In vivo ChIP analysis supports this notion, as despite the presence of the MBD and two functional AT-hooks in both MeCP2-G273X and MeCP2-R306C, the disruption of the basic cluster in MeCP2-R306C reduces binding to DNA even more than the complete absence of the cluster in MeCP2-G273X (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: R306 has an influence on DNA binding itself in addition to its role in NCoR complex binding.
source: R306 therefore has an influence on DNA binding itself in addition to its role in NCoR complex binding, and having a defective C-terminus (R306C) is worse than having no C-terminus at all.
evidence: This is inferred from ChIP and EMSA data showing R306C reduces DNA binding.

claim: Having a defective C-terminus (R306C) is worse than having no C-terminus at all.
source: R306 therefore has an influence on DNA binding itself in addition to its role in NCoR complex binding, and having a defective C-terminus (R306C) is worse than having no C-terminus at all.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of R306C and G273X phenotypes and DNA binding data.

claim: If excessive MeCP2 disrupts neuronal function by diverting corepressors away from loci they normally repress, then abolishing methyl-CpG binding in an extra copy of MeCP2 that is still capable of interacting with corepressors would still produce the duplication phenotype in mice.
source: If excessive MeCP2 disrupts neuronal function by diverting corepressors away from loci they normally repress, then abolishing methyl-CpG binding in an extra copy of MeCP2 that is still capable of interacting with corepressors (as we show in this study) would still produce the duplication phenotype in mice.
evidence: This is a hypothetical scenario used to test a mechanism.

claim: Overabundant MeCP2 does not exert toxic effects because it diverts corepressors away from their normal binding sites.
source: Instead, the R111G Tg mice were indistinguishable from wild-type mice. Therefore, overabundant MeCP2 does not exert toxic effects because it diverts corepressors away from their normal binding sites: rather, trouble arises when more abundant MeCP2 occupies more methyl-CpGs.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of phenotypes in R111G Tg mice despite retained corepressor binding.

claim: Trouble arises when more abundant MeCP2 occupies more methyl-CpGs.
source: Instead, the R111G Tg mice were indistinguishable from wild-type mice. Therefore, overabundant MeCP2 does not exert toxic effects because it diverts corepressors away from their normal binding sites: rather, trouble arises when more abundant MeCP2 occupies more methyl-CpGs.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of phenotypes in R111G Tg mice which cannot bind methyl-CpGs.

claim: The centrality of methyl-CpG binding to MeCP2 function was underscored by the R111G mice, which phenocopied the early lethality of the Mecp2 null mice.
source: The centrality of methyl-CpG binding to MeCP2 function was underscored by the R111G mice, which phenocopied the early lethality of the Mecp2 null mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival data showing R111G mice die as early as null mice.

claim: Lack of methyl-CpG binding leads to RTT.
source: All of this is consistent with studies asserting that lack of methyl-CpG binding leads to RTT (Kudo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A functional TRD is as necessary for the toxic effects of MeCP2 duplication as a functional MBD.
source: Like the R111G Tg mice, the R306C Tg mice were also indistinguishable from WT mice, demonstrating that a functional TRD is as necessary for the toxic effects of MeCP2 duplication as a functional MBD.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of phenotypes in both R111G Tg and R306C Tg mice.

claim: The R306C mice recapitulated many phenotypes seen in RTT patients, such as increased anxiety, motor dysfunction, and learning and memory deficits.
source: The R306C mice, though displaying milder phenotypes than Mecp2 null mice, recapitulated many phenotypes seen in RTT patients, such as increased anxiety, motor dysfunction, and learning and memory deficits (Hagberg et al., 1983; Chahrour and Zoghbi, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from R306C mice and comparison to clinical knowledge.

claim: The R306C allele must have an additional compromised function beyond its inability to bind NCoR through its TRD.
source: Because the G273X mouse model, which lacks the entire MeCP2 C-terminus, has a median survival of 28 weeks (Baker et al., 2013)—longer than both our R306C transgenic and the recently published R306C knock-in (median survival 18 weeks, this study, Lyst et al., 2013)—we hypothesized that the R306C allele must have an additional compromised function beyond its inability to bind NCoR through its TRD.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on comparison of survival data between R306C and G273X mice.

claim: MeCP2-R306C has reduced affinity for MeCP2 binding sequences in vivo, likely due to the disruption of a highly conserved basic cluster of amino acids (304-309) flanking R306, rendering it unable to bind DNA.
source: Indeed, we found that MeCP2-R306C has reduced affinity for MeCP2 binding sequences in vivo, likely due to the disruption of a highly conserved basic cluster of amino acids (304-309) flanking R306, rendering it unable to bind DNA.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP and EMSA data showing reduced DNA binding.

claim: The basic cluster flanking R306 has an additional function in binding DNA.
source: This study has added to our understanding of MeCP2 function by discovering that the basic cluster flanking R306 has an additional function in binding DNA and that this binding is abolished when basic residues in the cluster are mutated to neutral or acidic residues.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by EMSA data.

claim: DNA binding by the basic cluster flanking R306 is abolished when basic residues in the cluster are mutated to neutral or acidic residues.
source: This study has added to our understanding of MeCP2 function by discovering that the basic cluster flanking R306 has an additional function in binding DNA and that this binding is abolished when basic residues in the cluster are mutated to neutral or acidic residues.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data showing R306C, R306H, and K304E mutations abolish DNA binding.

claim: The R306C mutation is even more detrimental than lacking the entire basic cluster.
source: Moreover, the R306C mutation is even more detrimental than lacking the entire basic cluster.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of survival and ChIP data between R306C and G273X.

claim: An arginine to histidine disruption of the AT-hook in SOB3 produced a more severely impaired phenotype than a truncating mutation, indicating that the missense mutation has a dominant-negative effect on the function of the protein.
source: This is reminiscent of a study documenting loss-of-function mutations in SOB3, a gene encoding an AT-hook-containing protein. The authors showed that an arginine to histidine disruption of the AT-hook produced a more severely impaired phenotype than a truncating mutation, indicating that the missense mutation has a dominant-negative effect on the function of the protein (Street et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on SOB3.

claim: Mutation of R306 to either a cysteine or a histidine could have a dominant-negative effect on MeCP2 function.
source: Mutation of R306 to either a cysteine or a histidine could have the same dominant-negative effect.
evidence: This is speculated based on analogy to SOB3 and the observation that R306C is more detrimental than G273X.

claim: The region around R306 is a domain essential for MeCP2 function.
source: Uncovering a role for this basic cluster adds the region around R306 to the MBD, TRD, and AT-hooks as domains known to be essential for MeCP2 function.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional data showing the importance of the basic cluster.

claim: Comparisons of mouse lines carrying individual disease-causing mutations provide great insights into the function of MeCP2 and the pathogenesis of RTT.
source: In sum, comparisons of mouse lines carrying individual disease-causing mutations provide great insights into the function of MeCP2 and the pathogenesis of RTT.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: The PAC clone PAC671D9 was used to create the MECP2 duplication mouse model and predict the human disease.
source: This PAC clone was used to create the MECP2 duplication mouse model and predict the human disease, and on a Mecp2 null background it rescues loss-of-function phenotypes (Collins et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: PAC671D9 on a Mecp2 null background rescues loss-of-function phenotypes.
source: This PAC clone was used to create the MECP2 duplication mouse model and predict the human disease, and on a Mecp2 null background it rescues loss-of-function phenotypes (Collins et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: PAC671D9 has reliably produced founders with protein levels and expression pattern similar to that of endogenous MeCP2.
source: This PAC has reliably produced founders with protein levels and expression pattern similar to that of endogenous MeCP2 (Collins et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Doubling MeCP2 consistently causes phenotypes similar to the human MECP2 duplication syndrome.
source: Because doubling MeCP2 consistently causes phenotypes similar to the human syndrome, we chose one line (Line 1) of each mutant for further characterization (Collins et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.
